items.title: Section: Three Kinds of Expressed Karma — What Body, Speech, and Mind Each Make Visible

items.zh: 復次，云何表業？謂略有三種。一、染污，二、善，三、無記。若於身語意十不善業道，不離現行增上力故，所有身語表業，名染污表業。若即於彼誓受遠離，所有身語表業，名善表業。若諸威儀路工巧處一分，所有身語表業，名無記
items.en:
The Chapter of Deciding Discernment on the Five Sense-Consciousness-Corresponding Ground and the Mind Ground, part three.
Second, expressed and unexpressed karma; first, expressed karma; first, distinguishing its kinds; first, the question posed. Furthermore, what is expressed karma?
Second, the explanation; first, stating and listing. In brief, it is of three kinds: first, defiled; second, wholesome; third, neutral.
Second, explaining each; first, bodily and verbal expressed karma; first, defiled. Whenever bodily and verbal expressed karma manifests without departing from the force of the ten unwholesome courses of action of body, speech, and mind, this is called defiled expressed karma.
Second, wholesome. Whenever bodily and verbal expressed karma manifests through a vow to abandon these, this is called wholesome expressed karma.
Third, neutral. Whenever bodily and verbal expressed karma belongs to a portion of ordinary deportment or skilled craft, this is called neutral expressed karma.

items.title: Section: Mental Expressed Karma — The Volition That Moves the Mind Towards, Away From, or Simply Alongside Its Object

items.zh: 表業。若有不欲表示於他，唯自起心內意思擇，不說語言，但發善、染污、無記法現行意表業，名意表業。此中唯
items.en: Second, mental expressed karma. Whenever a person has no wish to express something to another, and simply gives rise, within their own mind, to reflective deliberation, without speaking any word, manifesting only wholesome, defiled, or neutral phenomena internally, this is called mental expressed karma.

items.title: Section: No Body Ever Truly Moves From One Place to Another — Expressed Karma Is Entirely Provisional

items.zh: 有身餘處滅於餘處生，或即此處唯變異生，名身表業；唯有語音，名語表業；唯有發起心造作思，名意表業。何以故？由一切行皆剎那故，從其餘方徙至餘方，不應道理。又離唯諸行生，餘實作用，由眼、耳、意皆不可得。是故當知一切表業皆是假有。
items.en:
Second, explaining the reason; first, refuting real motion. Why is this so? Because all conditioned phenomena are momentary, it is unreasonable to speak of moving from one place to another.
Second, revealing that only conditioned phenomena are found. Apart from the mere arising of conditioned phenomena, no further real function can be found, since neither the eye, the ear, nor the mind can ever locate one.
Third, concluding it is merely provisional. Therefore one should know that all expressed karma is merely provisionally existent.

items.title: Section: Born Into a Family of Butchers and Executioners — How an Unwholesome Vow Actually Takes Hold

items.zh: 復次，若有生不律儀家，有所了別自發期心，謂我當以此活命事而自活命；又於此活命事重復起心，欲樂忍可；爾時說名不律儀者。
items.en: Second, unexpressed karma; first, distinguishing its characteristics individually; first, subsumed under an unwholesome vow; first, arising from unwholesome intention; first, forming an expectant aspiration; first, taking up the case of one born into a family of unwholesome vow; first, explaining the name "one of unwholesome vow." Furthermore, if someone is born into a family of unwholesome vow, and, recognising this, spontaneously forms the intention, "I shall sustain my life through this very livelihood" — and further, with regard to this livelihood, again gives rise to the thought, taking delight in and consenting to it — at that time, this person is called one of unwholesome vow.

items.title: Section: Merely Resolving Is Already Unwholesome — And the Two Nuns Swindled Out of Eighty Million

items.zh: 由不律儀所攝故，極重不如理作意損害心所攝故，但成廣大諸不善根；然未成就殺生所生，及餘不善業道所生諸不善業，乃至所期事未現行。後若現行，若少若多，隨其所應，更復成就諸不善業。如生不律儀家，如是隨是何人、隨由何事起決猛心，廣說應知。
items.en:
Second, accomplishing broad unwholesome roots. Because one is subsumed under an unwholesome vow, subsumed under an exceptionally forceful, improper attention and a harmful mind, one thereby accomplishes broad unwholesome roots — yet has not yet accomplished the unwholesome karma arising from killing or the other unwholesome courses of action, since the intended deed has not yet been carried out.
Third, accomplishing unwholesome karma itself. Afterwards, if this is carried out, whether to a lesser or greater degree, one accordingly comes to accomplish unwholesome karma as well.
Second, extending this to every other circumstance. As with one born into a family of unwholesome vow, so too should it be understood in full for whatever person, through whatever circumstance, gives rise to this same fierce, resolute intention.

items.title: Section: Misfortune Compounds Daily Until Renounced — The Chan Master Who Freed an Empress With a Few Words

items.zh: 此人乃至不律儀思未捨已來，常得說名不律儀者。於日日分，彼不善思廣積集故，彼不善業多現行故，當知非福運運增長。
items.en: Second, clarifying the growth of demerit. This person continues to be called one of unwholesome vow for as long as this unwholesome intention remains unabandoned. Day after day, their unwholesome thoughts accumulate ever more broadly, and their unwholesome deeds manifest ever more often — one should know that their lack of merit correspondingly grows without pause.

items.title: Section: Five Companions of an Evil Resolve, and a Chinese Ledger of Merit That Extended a Dying Man's Life by Fifty Years

items.zh: 懈怠、忘念、散亂、惡慧俱行，能受彼業、能發彼業。從此已後，由種子故及現行故，處相續中現在轉時，名不律儀者。乃至由捨因緣未捨未棄。此中，若於惡業後不愛果，不信、不解、亦不隨入，是名不信。若隨所欲，於彼惡業憙樂而轉，不能勤勵息滅彼業，是名懈怠。若與過失相應，於有罪法不能如實明記有罪，是名忘念。若散亂染污心相續，不安住轉，是名散亂。若顛倒心相續而轉，於諸過失見勝功德，是名惡慧。由惡尸羅增上力故，所有不善思俱行不善不信等現在轉時，名惡戒者。
items.en:
Second, laziness. Indulging one's own desire towards an unwholesome deed, taking delight in it, while failing to diligently strive to extinguish it, is called laziness.
Third, forgetfulness. Being joined with fault yet failing to genuinely remember it as a fault is called forgetfulness.
Fourth, distraction. A defiled mind continuing restlessly, never settling, is called distraction.
Fifth, corrupted wisdom. An inverted mind continuing on, perceiving superior merit within one's own faults, is called corrupted wisdom.
Third, by bad conduct. Sustained by the force of habitually bad conduct, when unwholesome intention manifests together with faithlessness and the rest, this is called one of bad conduct.

items.title: Section: The Wholesome Vow Begins — Why Only a Buddha or a Pratyekabuddha May Ordain Themselves

items.zh: 若與此相違，如其所應，當知得有律儀隨轉。差別者，謂有堪受律儀方可得受。此中或有由他、由自而受律儀，或復有一唯自然受，除苾芻律儀。何以故？由苾芻律儀非一切堪受故。若苾芻律儀非要從他受者，若堪出家、若不堪出家，但欲出家者，便應一切隨其所欲，自然出家。如是聖教便無軌範，亦無善說法毘柰耶而可了知。是故苾芻律儀無有自然受義。
items.en:
Second, subsumed under a wholesome vow; first, contrasting it with the opposite. Whoever is opposed to this, appropriately accompanied by faith and the rest, should be known to have an active wholesome vow.
Second, revealing its distinctions; first, clarifying its reception; first, briefly stating it. The distinction is that only one genuinely capable of receiving the vow may actually receive it.
Second, explaining each; first, distinguishing the modes. Some receive this vow through another and through themselves, and one case — apart from monastic precepts — may be received spontaneously.
Second, explaining the reason; first, received only through another; first, stating this is not otherwise. Why is this so? Because not everyone is capable of receiving the monastic precepts.
Second, explaining the fault. If monastic precepts were not necessarily received through another, then whether qualified or unqualified, anyone who simply wished to ordain would do so as they pleased, and the sacred teaching would then have no order at all, with no properly transmitted discipline left to learn. Therefore monastic precepts admit no spontaneous reception.

items.title: Section: Shame and Conscience — Why a Precept Received From Another Still Needs One's Own Sincere Vow

items.zh: 問：若除苾芻律儀，所餘律儀有自然受者，何因緣故復從他受？答：由有二種遠離惡戒受隨護支，所謂慚、愧。若於他處及於自處現行罪時，深生羞恥，如是於離惡戒受隨護支乃能具受，故從他受。若有慚正現前，必亦有愧，非有愧者必定有慚，是故慚法最為強勝。
items.en:
Second, receiving through both self and other; first, the question. Question: apart from monastic precepts, since other precepts may be received spontaneously, why does one still receive them through another as well?
Second, the answer; first, distinguishing reception through another; first, stating it. Answer: because there are two supports that guard against bad conduct and sustain precept-keeping — namely, shame and conscience.
Second, explaining this. Whenever fault manifests in relation to oneself or another, and one gives rise to deep shame because of it, one thereby becomes fully capable of guarding against bad conduct and sustaining the precepts — this is why one receives them through another.
Second, explaining self-administered reception; first, citing the more powerful cause. Whoever genuinely possesses shame invariably possesses conscience as well, though one who possesses conscience does not necessarily possess shame — therefore shame is the more powerful support.

blocks.text: Fascicle 53 discusses karma and vows. What makes a deed a deed? The Yogācāra answer: intention (volition). Even an unspoken resolve begins to shape a person.

Not departing from the ten unwholesome courses of action is defiled; vowing to abandon them is wholesome. Master Cháng Bǎi: what shows outwardly is "expressed" karma, with manifest volition as its substance; "unexpressed" karma has the seed of volition as its substance. Neither is a real material thing.
Master Cháng Bǎi: towards a pleasant object, volition moves the mind to join it; towards an unpleasant one, to separate; towards a neutral one, it simply goes along.
Because conditioned things are momentary, it is unreasonable to say something moves from one place to another; there is only the arising of things.

The name "butcher" attaches to intention, not to birth or a finished deed: the person intends to live this way and consents to it. Master Cháng Bǎi: though they have not yet acted, merely forming this intention already counts.
Through the vow and a harmful mind, broad unwholesome roots are formed, though not yet the karma of killing itself, until the deed is done.
Day after day unwholesome thoughts accumulate and demerit grows. Master Cháng Bǎi: whether a good or an evil thought, it is the same: the first thought, then gradual growth.
"Perceiving superior merit within one's own faults." Master Cháng Bǎi: holding that a fault has merit is corrupted wisdom.

subs.head: Why ordination is received from another

blocks.text: Otherwise anyone, qualified or not, would ordain at will, and the teaching would lose its order. Master Cháng Bǎi: another confers the precepts while one makes the vow oneself.
Master Cháng Bǎi: shame is resolving not to do wrong even when alone; conscience is answering to others, to protect their faith.
"Whether a good or an evil thought, it is the same: first one thought, then it grows." This works in both directions, and that is the point of practice.

quiz.q: How are the defiled, wholesome, and neutral kinds of bodily and verbal expressed karma distinguished?
options: not departing from the ten unwholesome courses is defiled; a vow to abandon them is wholesome; a portion of deportment or craft is neutral
committing the ten unwholesome courses is neutral; a vow to abandon them is wholesome; a portion of deportment or craft is always defiled
by the result they bring: an evil destiny is defiled, a good destiny wholesome, and no result neutral
by the three doors: bodily karma is defiled, verbal karma neutral, and mental karma wholesome
quiz.why: The treatise sorts expressed karma by its relation to the ten unwholesome courses of action: not departing from them is defiled, vowing to abandon them is wholesome, and a portion of ordinary deportment or skilled craft is neutral. Master Cháng Bǎi: when one vows to abandon the ten courses, the matching movement of body and speech at that moment is wholesome expressed karma.

quiz.q: What does Master Cháng Bǎi give as the substance of expressed karma and of unexpressed karma?
options: expressed karma has the seed of volition as its substance; unexpressed karma has manifesting volition
expressed karma has the real form of bodily and verbal movement; unexpressed karma has karmic form made of particles
both have the store-consciousness itself as their substance and differ only in name
expressed karma has manifesting volition as its substance; unexpressed karma has the seed of volition
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: what shows outwardly is called expressed karma, and all of it has manifesting volition as its substance; unexpressed karma is karma not shown outwardly, and it has the seed of volition as its substance. So neither is a real physical thing, which prepares the conclusion that all expressed karma is provisional.

quiz.q: Mental expressed karma is inward deliberation. How does Master Cháng Bǎi say volition moves the mind towards the three kinds of object?
options: from the agreeable it separates; towards the disagreeable it joins; with what is neither, it receives the object's image
towards all three it joins the mind with the object, only the feeling differing
it moves the mind towards none of them; volition acts only at the moment of speaking
towards the agreeable it joins with the object; from the disagreeable it separates; with the neither it receives the object's image
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: when an agreeable object brings pleasant feeling, volition moves the mind to join with the object; when a disagreeable object brings painful feeling, volition moves the mind to separate from it; when an object neither agreeable nor disagreeable brings neutral feeling, volition moves the mind to receive the object's image. Such inward activity, shown to no one, is mental expressed karma.

quiz.q: Why does the treatise conclude that all expressed karma is provisionally existent?
options: all conditioned phenomena are momentary, so moving from place to place is unreasonable; apart from their arising no real function is found
bodily and verbal movement depends on the elements, which are impermanent, so movement is not real
expressed karma is visible only to others and not to oneself, so it is called provisional
expressed karma brings no result; only unexpressed karma does, so expressed karma is provisional
quiz.why: Because all conditioned phenomena are momentary, the treatise says it is unreasonable to speak of something moving from one place to another; and apart from the mere arising of phenomena, no further real function can be found. Master Cháng Bǎi: the various marks of bodily expression are only provisionally designated upon conditioned phenomena arising and ceasing moment by moment.

quiz.q: At what point is someone born into a family of unwholesome vow called "one of unwholesome vow"?
options: when they themselves form the intention to live by this livelihood, and again delight in and consent to it
from the moment of birth into such a family, whatever they intend
only when they actually kill, completing the first full course of action, and not before then
when they undergo a formal rite of bad precepts and enter the trade
quiz.why: The treatise ties the name to intention, not to birth or to a finished deed: the person forms the intention to live by this livelihood and again delights in and consents to it. Master Cháng Bǎi: though this person has not yet acted, merely agreeing at heart that this occupation is right already makes them one of unwholesome vow.

quiz.q: Before the intended deed is carried out, what has this person accomplished, and what not yet?
options: they have accomplished the unwholesome karma arising from killing and the rest, but not yet the broad unwholesome roots
both roots and karma are accomplished, and only the ripened result has yet to appear
they have accomplished only broad unwholesome roots, not yet the unwholesome karma arising from killing and the rest
neither roots nor karma are accomplished, since it is all only in the mind
quiz.why: The treatise separates two stages. Through the vow and a harmful mind one accomplishes broad unwholesome roots, yet not the unwholesome karma arising from killing and the other courses, until the intended deed is carried out. Master Cháng Bǎi: at this point there is only such a seed and such a thought in the mind. Once carried out, unwholesome karma is accomplished as well.

quiz.q: How does the treatise define "corrupted wisdom"?
options: joined with fault, yet failing to remember it truly as a fault
an inverted mind continuing on, perceiving superior merit within faults
delighting in an unwholesome deed and failing to strive to extinguish it
a defiled, scattered mind continuing on, never settling
quiz.why: The treatise defines corrupted wisdom as an inverted mind continuing on, perceiving superior merit within one's own faults. Master Cháng Bǎi: holding that a fault has superior merit is corrupted wisdom. The other options are the treatise's definitions of forgetfulness, laziness, and distraction, which accompany an evil resolve in the same passage.

quiz.q: The treatise says demerit grows without pause until the unwholesome intention is abandoned. How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain this?
options: it grows only on days of actual evil and stays level on other days
the result is received all at once and the karma is cleared, which merely makes demerit look as if it grows
there is a first thought and then gradual growth; the seed infused continues on, seed producing seed
demerit is recorded daily by guardian spirits, and the figure rises with the days
quiz.why: The treatise says that day after day unwholesome thoughts accumulate and deeds manifest, so demerit grows. Master Cháng Bǎi: whether a good thought or an evil one, it is the same: first comes the first thought, and then it gradually grows; the seed infused keeps continuing, seed producing seed. So the growth does not depend on the outward deed alone.

quiz.q: Why does the treatise say monastic precepts admit no spontaneous reception?
options: because the merit of spontaneous reception is too small to fulfil a monastic's virtue
because spontaneous reception existed only in the Buddha's lifetime and ended with his passing
because shame and conscience can be gained only from a teacher, not from oneself
if reception from another were not required, the qualified and unqualified alike would ordain at will, and the teaching would have no order
quiz.why: The treatise reasons from what would follow: if monastic precepts were not necessarily received through another, anyone wishing to ordain, qualified or not, would do so at will, and the sacred teaching would have no order. Master Cháng Bǎi: if anyone who wished to ordain were simply allowed to, Buddhism would have no standard and no rule.

quiz.q: The English has "Some receive this vow through another, some through themselves alone." How does Master Cháng Bǎi read this, and what is the problem with the English?
options: through another means lay precepts and through oneself monastic precepts; the English "alone" is correct, needs no change, and fits the next line
through another and through oneself are one case: another confers it and one also vows; "alone" splits them and confuses it with spontaneous reception
through another means monks' precepts and through oneself nuns'; the English "vow" blurs the two
both are other names for spontaneous reception; "through another" is wrong and all should read "alone"
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: receiving through another and through oneself means another confers the precepts while one makes the vow oneself, with a preceptor and others as witnesses. So the two are a single case, set against spontaneous reception. The English "some through themselves alone" makes three modes, and "alone" has no basis in the Chinese.

quiz.q: Since other precepts may be received spontaneously, why does one still receive them through another?
options: because the merit of reception through another exceeds that of spontaneous reception
because spontaneous reception lasts only a day and night, and longer needs another
because there can be no vow without bodily and verbal expression
because shame and conscience support abandoning bad conduct; deep shame before others and oneself makes full reception possible
quiz.why: The treatise answers that there are two supports for abandoning bad conduct and sustaining the precepts: shame and conscience. Fault manifesting before oneself or another gives rise to deep shame, and so one receives through another. Master Cháng Bǎi: only a deep feeling of shame before oneself and others gives the strength to leave evil conduct and to receive and keep the precepts. Merit is not the reason, for the treatise says it does not differ.

quiz.q: "Whoever has shame has conscience, but not necessarily the reverse." How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain this?
options: shame means not doing evil even alone; conscience means answering to others; one with conscience alone may feel no inner shame
shame means answering to others; conscience means not doing evil even alone; one with shame alone may ignore others' faith
shame arises at ordination and conscience after a lapse, so shame comes first
shame belongs only to noble ones and conscience to ordinary beings as well
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: shame means resolving by oneself not to do evil even when alone; conscience means answering to others, in order to protect their pure faith. One with conscience alone may only fear wronging others when at fault, without feeling inner shame. That is why the treatise calls shame the more powerful support for one who receives the precepts by oneself.
